query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating advanced free‐energy sampling methods (e.g., metadynamics or umbrella sampling) with machine learning–accelerated interatomic potentials can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across the high‐entropy alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloys in their solid phase at temperatures approaching melting, featuring complex multi‐component, disordered atomic arrangements.
generation.intervention: Implement an advanced free‐energy calculation framework by coupling metadynamics or umbrella sampling with machine learning–optimized interatomic potentials calibrated against high‐fidelity ab initio data and benchmark calorimetry.
generation.conditions: Equilibrium high-temperature conditions near the melting point across a broad range of HEA compositions. The system is thermally equilibrated in simulations and experimentally measured using high-sensitivity DSC techniques.
generation.structural_mediator: The identification and tracking of well‐defined order parameters that capture the progression of atomic disorder during melting mediate the transition in the free‐energy landscape.
generation.mechanism: By systematically sampling the full free‐energy landscape of the solid–liquid transformation, the energy barriers and changes in structural order are integrated to yield quantitative estimates of melting temperature, latent heat (enthalpy of fusion), entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting. These computed thermodynamic properties are validated against experimental calorimetric data.
generation.predicted_outcome: The framework will converge to melting temperatures and associated fusion thermodynamics with an expected accuracy improvement over conventional DSC or CALPHAD methods—potentially within a 5–10% relative error margin—thereby delineating the liquid‐phase properties in a computationally efficient manner across diverse HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Existing experimental data from high-sensitivity DSC measurements and first‐principles molecular dynamics simulations on selected HEA systems serve as calibration references.
generation.boundary: The method may face limitations for alloys with extremely complex or metastable phase landscapes if the machine learning potentials are insufficiently trained or if the chosen order parameters do not fully capture the local structural changes during melting.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary estimates suggest an accuracy improvement to within 5–10% relative to experimental DSC measurements, uncertainties remain regarding the universal transferability of the machine learning potentials and the sampling efficiency in capturing rare-event transitions in very complex HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of HEA compositions covering a broad compositional space. For each alloy, calculate the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change using the advanced free‐energy framework and compare with high‐sensitivity differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) experiments performed under matched conditions.
measurements: Fusion entropy (derived from DSC data and temperature)
Volume change (measured by dilatometry or in situ high-temperature X-ray/neutron scattering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across a statistically significant number of HEA compositions, the computed values deviate by more than approximately 10% consistently from the experimental measurements (adjusted for known experimental uncertainties), then the advanced free‐energy sampling approach would be ruled out as inadequate for accurate thermodynamic prediction in HEAs.

The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are multi-principal element alloys that exhibit complex multi-phase behavior at elevated temperatures approaching melting.
frame.goal: To accurately and efficiently determine key melting-related properties: melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change upon melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for the HEA family.
frame.limitation: Existing methods often struggle with the complexity and compositional diversity of HEAs, resulting in inefficiencies or inaccuracies in capturing thermodynamic phase transition details across a broad compositional space.
root_cause_cues: decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach
constraints: The approach must provide a sound physical rationale based on thermodynamic principles.
Expected quantitative performance metrics (accuracy, resolution) need to be clearly defined.
The method should have a wide range of applicability across different HEA compositions.
Supporting prior experimental or modeling evidence is required.
It must include a validation benchmark that could decisively falsify the method if it fails.
frame.regime: High temperature conditions near the melting point, encompassing both the solid–liquid transition and properties of the liquid state under thermal equilibrium.
prior_attempts: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), which can be limited by sensitivity and resolution issues in complex multi-component systems.
Computational thermodynamics approaches such as CALPHAD, which struggle with predictive accuracy for novel HEAs.
First-principles molecular dynamics simulations that, while detailed, are often computationally expensive and limited in statistical sampling for HEA systems.

decision.trend: Across the past decade, research on HEAs has advanced from proving high‐temperature phase stability and mechanical performance (using conventional melting, casting, and annealing techniques) toward employing high‐throughput synthesis and in situ characterization methods under extreme conditions. Early studies focused on processing–structure–property relationships at high temperature, while more recent work on refractory and rapidly solidified HEAs has increasingly raised the challenge of capturing transient thermodynamic details. Yet, none of these studies directly tackled the accurate determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, liquid-phase thermodynamic properties, or volume change at fusion due to limitations in experimental sensitivity (as seen with DSC) and in the predictive power of conventional computational approaches (e.g., CALPHAD or brute-force first-principles MD).
decision.unsolved: A robust, physically grounded method capable of accurately and efficiently mapping the solid–liquid transformation thermodynamics in high-entropy alloys across a broad compositional space is still missing. Specifically, an approach is needed that delivers quantitative metrics (melting temperature, latent heat, entropy, and volume change) with clearly defined resolution and accuracy, along with a decisive experimental/computational validation benchmark to falsify the method if it lacks predictive accuracy.
decision.lever: Develop an advanced free-energy calculation framework—such as integrating metadynamics or umbrella sampling with machine learning–accelerated interatomic potentials—to compute the complete free-energy landscape of the solid–liquid transition in HEAs. The key parameters would include well‐defined order parameters for melting, rigorous thermodynamic integration, and systematic calibration against benchmark experiments (e.g., high-sensitivity DSC measurements) to decisively validate the computed fusion properties.
decision.why: This step directly follows the trend of moving from traditional high-temperature processing and microstructural characterization toward reliable, physics‐based computational methods that can surmount the inherent challenges posed by compositional complexity. By leveraging advanced sampling techniques and surrogate models, the approach promises both accuracy and efficiency, while its built-in validation criterion (a decisive mismatch with high-resolution calorimetry) would conclusively rule out the method if it fails to capture the underlying thermodynamic behavior.
